A message sent in seconds can stay with someone all day.
Cyberbullying is using messages, games, social media or other digital tools to hurt, threaten or embarrass someone.
Cyberbullying can happen publicly, in private messages or through a fake account.
The effects can carry into school, friendships and daily life.

blocks.heading: Why we made this issue
blocks.body: We talk, play and learn online. Those spaces feel better when everyone can take part without being mocked, threatened or left out.

blocks.heading: What we’ll cover
blocks.body: We’ll look at what cyberbullying looks like, why it hurts, and what a student can do when it happens to them or to a friend. Online harm grows when bystanders join in. Staying silent can leave the person feeling alone, while a quiet check-in can show that someone noticed.

blocks.heading: A school group chat
blocks.body: Imagine a student’s photo being turned into a joke and forwarded between groups. More people see it each time it’s shared, and the student may feel followed by the joke even after school.

blocks.heading: Respectful disagreement
blocks.body: Two classmates can disagree about a game or a school project. Mocking someone, sharing their private messages or encouraging others to pile on is harmful. A single post can still cause repeated harm if it keeps being copied or shared. Take threats seriously and show them to a trusted adult.

blocks.heading: Harassment
blocks.body: Sending insults or threats, or repeatedly mocking someone in comments.

blocks.heading: Rumours and privacy
blocks.body: Spreading a false story or posting photos, screenshots or personal details without permission to embarrass someone.

blocks.heading: Impersonation and exclusion
blocks.body: Creating a fake profile in someone’s name, or deliberately excluding them from a group to humiliate them. Examples include leaving cruel voice notes after a game, forwarding a private screenshot, or messaging classmates from a fake profile.

blocks.heading: Feelings and friendships
blocks.body: Someone might feel embarrassed or anxious, stop joining group conversations or find it harder to trust friends.

blocks.heading: Learning and rest
blocks.body: Worry about the next message can make it harder to focus in class or settle down at night.

blocks.heading: Support matters
blocks.body: Listening calmly and helping someone speak to a trusted adult can make it easier for them to ask for help. Students react in different ways. A friend who suddenly goes quiet in a familiar group may need someone to check in privately.

blocks.heading: A screenshot can be evidence
blocks.body: If it’s safe to do so, save a screenshot privately with the account name and time visible. Show it to a trusted adult or use it to report the post.

blocks.heading: A private message can help
blocks.body: A short message like “I saw what happened. I’m here if you want to talk” can help a classmate feel supported. If the content is upsetting or private, avoid making extra copies. Ask an adult to help you preserve only what’s needed for a report.

blocks.heading: 1. Pause
blocks.body: Step away and avoid replying with insults.

blocks.heading: 2. Save and report
blocks.body: Keep evidence privately when safe. Block or mute the account and report the harmful content in the app.

blocks.heading: 3. Tell someone
blocks.body: Speak with a trusted adult, such as a parent, teacher or school counsellor. If it happens to a friend, check in privately. If there’s an immediate threat, tell a trusted adult right away. A student shouldn’t have to handle it alone.

blocks.heading: Check in privately
blocks.body: Ask whether they want to talk or would like you to go with them to a teacher they trust.

blocks.heading: Stop the spread
blocks.body: Avoid sharing or reacting to the harmful post, and report it if you can.

blocks.heading: Psychological and educational guidance
blocks.body: She led an awareness activity as head of the Psychological Counseling and Educational Guidance Unit at Al-Mustaqbal University’s College of Education in Iraq.

blocks.heading: An article on bullying among teens
blocks.body: She wrote about how bullying, including cyberbullying, affects teenagers and discussed how schools and families can help prevent it and support students.

blocks.heading: A talk on violence among peers
blocks.body: She spoke at an Al-Mustaqbal University event in March 2025 about forms of violence among teenagers, including cyberbullying.
